title: Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue

Every member of Wall Street's "Magnificent Seven" now wants its stock kept off OKX and ICE's planned tokenized stock venue.

Apple and Meta Platforms are among 11 companies added to the list of objecting issuers in an updated notice from OKXICE TSV dated Thursday.

They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla, completing a sweep by the group of tech giants that makes up a large share of the S&P 500's value. The other new objectors are Home Depot, Boeing, GE Vernova, Palantir, ServiceNow, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Nebius Group, bringing the total number of companies saying "no" to the OKX and ICE platform to 67.

Meta's objection carries some irony. The Facebook parent once tried to launch its own stablecoin, Libra, later renamed Diem, before abandoning the project in 2022 amid regulatory pushback.

Apple had been one of the last megacaps missing from the list after Amazon, Tesla, and SpaceX objected in the venue's Nov. 2 notice. The tally stood at 56 then, and at nine on Oct. 15, when the first objectors appeared.

Just as notable is who hasn't objected. Crypto-friendly public companies such as Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy don't appear on the list. Coinbase launched tokenized stocks for non-U.S. users on its Base network in August. Berkshire Hathaway, Visa, and Exxon Mobil are also absent. It's unclear whether OKXICE notified those companies.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. It's worth noting, though, that the objection applies only to that venue.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to offer tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain. An outside "tokenizer" would hold real shares one-for-one through a registered broker-dealer.

With the market's biggest names opted out, it's unclear which major stocks the venue will be able to offer at launch, and its notices don't list the tokens it plans to make available.

Snowflake (SNOW) stock gained 56.8% between February 9 and November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 6.8% over the same dates. The rise was not steady. The stock recorded its two largest one-day gains of that stretch in the sessions immediately following the company's quarterly reports on May 27 and September 2. Those two days alone added more than the whole rise, and the shares have since fallen from a high close of $368.89 on October 9 to $275.88 on November 6. Your view of this move turns on how fast sales are growing and how much more buyers now pay for those sales while Snowflake still loses money. What did Snowflake report just before those two days?

What Snowflake Reported In May And September

On May 27, Snowflake reported product revenue of $1.33 billion for fiscal Q1 2027, up 34% from a year earlier. The shares rose 36.5% the next day, marking the largest one-session gain of the whole rise.

On September 2, the company reported fiscal Q2 2027 product revenue of $1.49 billion, up 37% from a year earlier. Management called it the third straight quarter in which product revenue growth sped up, and the stock added 16.6% the following session.

How Much Of Snowflake's Business Is Growing Faster?

Nearly all of it: product revenue made up 95.5% of Snowflake's sales in fiscal 2026, so faster product growth is, in effect, faster growth for the whole company. Total revenue growth rose in each quarter from 28.7% in fiscal Q3 2026 to 35.1% in fiscal Q2 2027.

Management said on the September 2 call that newer AI products contributed about half of the speed-up in product growth. Management also raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for product revenue to $6.07 billion, which would be 36% growth.

Losses narrowed as well. Snowflake's operating loss equaled 17.0% of revenue in fiscal Q2 2027, compared with 29.7% in fiscal Q2 2026.

Snowflake Still Reports A Net Loss

Snowflake had a net loss of $1.09 billion over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, compared with $1.38 billion a year earlier. It reported a net loss in fiscal Q4 2026, which ended on January 31, 2026, before the rise began, and in both quarters since.

With no profit, Snowflake's price-to-earnings ratio is not meaningful. The stock trades at 17.7 times its sales, compared with 3.1 times for the S&P 500. At the end of March 2026, Snowflake's multiple was 10.4 times sales, so buyers now pay far more for each dollar of sales while the company still reports a loss.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock is under pressure despite another blowout quarterly performance, as investors zeroed in on a sharp slowdown in U.S. commercial bookings. The artificial intelligence (AI) software company reported third-quarter revenue of $2.31 billion, up 96% year-over-year (YOY), while U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% YOY to $984 million and surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time. Yet U.S. commercial total contract value (TCV) rose just 11% YOY to $1.46 billion, a steep deceleration from the 153% growth recorded in the prior quarter.

The slowdown has raised concerns about whether Palantir can sustain the extraordinary growth rates embedded in its premium valuation. While management attributed the weaker bookings growth partly to customers signing shorter-duration contracts, investors are watching closely to see whether those contracts translate into faster renewals and larger deals down the road. The cautious reaction is notable because Palantir also raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $8.53 billion to $8.534 billion and expects U.S. commercial revenue to grow at least 143%.

Palantir's Earnings Beat Wall Street Estimates

Palantir cleared both bars Wall Street set for the third quarter. The company reported adjusted EPS of $0.44 versus analysts' estimate of $0.41, while revenue of $2.31 billion beat the consensus estimate of $2.18 billion.

Palantir grew revenue 96% year-over-year (YOY) and surpassed $2 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time. On the Q3 earnings call, the company called it the highest growth it has ever posted as a public company. Palantir also reported net income of $1.13 billion, up from $476 million during the same period last year.

On the Q3 call, CFO David Glazer noted that adjusted operating margin stood at 62%, allowing Palantir to report an operating cash flow of $1.2 billion. The company ended the quarter with $10.4 billion in cash.

Glazer also cited the company's Rule of 40 score, which is a quick health check for software companies. The figure calculates whether a company is growing fast while making money by adding together its revenue growth rate and adjusted operating margin. Using Palantir's 96% YOY revenue growth and adjusted operating margin of 62%, the company earned a Rule of 40 score of 158% in Q3.

The usual benchmark for the score is 40%, and a score above that level is generally seen as healthy. Palantir's score of 158% is nearly four times that mark, which is why CEO Alex Karp called the number "jaw dropping" on the earnings call. Glazer also noted that the score rose three points from the prior quarter and confirmed that Q3 marked the 13th-straight quarter of improvement.

U.S. Commercial Revenue Passes Government Sales

Palantir built its name on government work, including support for U.S. warfighters. Commercial customers were once a side business. In Q3, however, U.S. commercial revenue accounted for the majority of sales.

Markets are trembling amid the latest AI stock sell-off, which has sent shares of major AI players deep into the red. But CNBC's Jim Cramer believes the downturn is not another dot-com crash.

Cramer warned that AI stocks could fall further, particularly semiconductor companies whose shares surged during the AI boom. However, he argued that unlike the speculative businesses that collapsed in 2000, many of today's AI companies are highly profitable.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) has been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence (AI) software revolution over the past three years, with the company's AI platform in solid demand from both commercial and government customers.

So, when Palantir released its third-quarter results on Nov. 2, it was easy to see why the company's revenue and earnings grew at an incredible pace. What's more, Palantir raised its full-year guidance once again, driven by the exceptional growth in the company's U.S. commercial business.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, Palantir stock slid following its earnings report. Let's see why that was the case and examine a potential red flag that could derail the company's impressive growth trajectory.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Palantir's quarterly performance was solid, but there is a problem

Palantir's Q3 revenue increased by 96% year over year to $2.3 billion. This was the first time its quarterly revenue crossed the $2 billion milestone. Even better, the company's adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increased by 109% year over year to $0.44. Palantir's revenue and earnings exceeded Wall Street's expectations.

Palantir benefited from the persistently strong demand for its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), which is helping it win more business from existing customers. Management pointed out several instances during the company's latest earnings call in which customers have awarded Palantir larger contracts following the initial deployment of its AI solutions.

For instance, Palantir noted that a "global athletic company converted a $1.6 million pilot that began in Q1 2026 into an approximately $21 million ACV deal last quarter," where ACV refers to the annual contract value. Management outlined several other examples, indicating that the benefits delivered by Palantir's AI software platform are boosting demand.

This also explains why Palantir increased its annual revenue guidance once again. It now expects $8.53 billion in revenue for 2026, driven by a 143% increase in U.S. commercial revenue to $3.56 billion. The updated guidance implies a 91% increase in Palantir's top line, which would be an improvement over its 2025 growth of 56%.

Meanwhile, the company anticipates adjusted free cash flow of $4.8-$5 billion this year, significantly higher than last year's $2.27 billion. So, there are a lot of positive takeaways from Palantir's latest quarterly report. However, a sharp slowdown in new contracts marred the company's impressive performance and strong guidance.
